description:
FILED s428 (Fable), found by the s427 review probes; PRE-EXISTING in the sense
that before s427 the whole `@?` family dropped, so the string shape was never
reachable — it is the interpolation twin of what s427 fixed in CODE.

    @? = (1,2,3);
    print $?[1], "\n";      # perl 2   PCL 2     (s427, (p-aref @? 1))
    print "$?[1]\n";        # perl 2   PCL 0[1]  <- this task
    "abc" =~ /b/; print "$-[0]:$+[0]\n";   # perl 1:2  PCL 1:2  (the @-/@+ twins WORK)

So StringInterpolation / Pl::InterpScan's `$` arm knows `$-[` and `$+[` as
element-of-magic-array but treats `$?` (and presumably `$!`, `$.`, `$/`, …)
as a scalar special that ENDS the reference, leaving the subscript literal.
perl's rule (toke.c, S_intuit_more-adjacent): after `$?` etc. a `[` starts
a subscript of the punctuation ARRAY — the same rule as `$-[0]`.

SILENT WRONG (the value is "0[1]", no diagnostic).  0 corpus rows (the only
`@?` row in four populations is t/re/subst.t:346, which is `! @?`, not an
interpolation).  Fix belongs in Pl/InterpScan.pm (standing rule §8: scanning
happens there or not at all), in the same arm that already handles `$-[`/`$+[`
— widen the class to the punctuation-array family s427's %PUNCT_ARRAY_CHARS
names, keeping `$#[` and the CL-unsafe names (#449) out.  Probe the breaking
case: `"$?[1]"` where @? is EMPTY still prints "" in perl (not "$?[1]" text),
and `"$? [1]"` (space) is the scalar then literal.

Guard: add a row to Pl/t/punct-array-glob-01.t beside s427's code-path rows.


=== s438h (Opus 5, 2026-08-23) DONE, in Pl/InterpScan.pm as the standing rule
requires (Â§8: interpolation scanning happens there or not at all), in the same
arm that already handled `$-[` / `$+[`.

`_scan_dollar`'s punctuation-magic arm continued into a subscript chain for `+`
and `-` ONLY, so every other punctuation name ENDED the reference and left the
subscript literal: `"$?[1]"` printed `0[1]` -- the scalar `$?` followed by the
text -- with no diagnostic.

THE SET WAS PROBED ONE CHARACTER AT A TIME against perl 5.40.3 (`@X =
(11,22,33); print "C:", $X[1], " S:$X[1]"`), and it is deliberately NOT
Pl::Parser's %PUNCT_ARRAY_CHARS:

    ? . / ~ & % = < >   perl C:22 S:22 -- in the set
    ^                   perl does NOT subscript: `$^` is the format-top-of-page
                        name and `"$^[1]"` leaves the bracket alone.  It IS in
                        Pl::Parser's set, because that one asks a different
                        question -- which characters can be EMITTED bare as a
                        CL symbol.  Two sets, two questions, both documented at
                        both ends.
    the CL-unsafe names (`@,` `@;` `@|` `@'` `@"` â¦) stay out for task #449's
                        reason: they need a pipe-quoted emission that does not
                        exist yet, so they keep dropping LOUDLY rather than
                        start half-working.

AFTER THE FIX, NINE OF THE TEN AGREE WITH PERL IN BOTH PATHS.  The tenth is
`!`, and it is wrong in the CODE path too (`$![1]` emits
`(p-aref (p-errno-string) 1)` -- the SCALAR `$!`, indexed): PRE-EXISTING,
verified on a cf0076c worktree, and filed as #487.  Before this change the two
paths disagreed (`S:[1]` vs `C:`), which is why only the string half looked
broken; now they agree, and agree wrongly, which is what makes it a task.

MEASURED: corpus-diff IDENTICAL over the 111; emission-ab over the four
populations = 951 files SAME / 0 DIFF / 0 RCDIFF (the only `@?` row in any
population is t/re/subst.t:346, `! @?`, not an interpolation); gate 166/5777;
full sweep TOTAL 18312 (+0), GATE clean.  Guard: two rows in
Pl/t/punct-array-glob-01.t (17 -> 19) -- one positive covering `$?[1]`,
`$.[2]`, `$/[0]`, the `@-`/`@+` twins and an out-of-range read, and one INVERSE
asserting that a SPACE ends the reference (`"$? [1]"` is the scalar then
literal text, as in perl).  Inverse-guarded on a cf0076c worktree: row 18 fails
there, 19 passes.
title: "$?[1]" / "$![0]" — a PUNCTUATION-named array's element inside a dq string interpolates the SCALAR `$?` and leaves `[1]` literal (perl: element 1 of @?)
